\( \def\R{\mathbb{R}} \)

MATH2010 Advanced Calculus I

Single-variable calculus are somewhat more simple. How about vector-valued multi-variable functions? Can we study rate of change, finding maximum / minimum and do approximations, say for function $f: \mathbb{R}^3 \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^2$ with $f(x, y, z) = (x + y, e^x)$? Well, we have to first define what a vector is in the Euclidean Space.

Euclidean Space

The Euclidean Space $\R^n = \R \times \R \times \cdots \times \R = \{ (x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n) : x_i \in \R \}$ is the set of points (or vectors) in the $n$-dimensional space. We also call the elements of $\R$ scalars. For points $A, B \in \R^n$, the vector $\overrightarrow{AB}$ is the vector from $A$ to $B$, where $\big\Vert \overrightarrow{AB} \big\Vert$ is the magnitude or norm of $\overrightarrow{AB}$.

Vector Operations

We may simply define vector operations such as equality, addition and scalar multiplication just normally. How to define length, area and volume in terms of vectors?

To incorporate the idea of length, we define dot product $a \cdot b = \sum a_i \cdot b_i$ for $a, b \in \R^n$. The euclidean norm of vector $a$ is just $\Vert a \Vert = \sqrt{a \cdot a}$. Alternatively, it can be represent as $\langle a, b \rangle$. We can derive two inequalities, the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, $| a \cdot b | \le \Vert a \Vert \cdot \Vert b \Vert$ and the triangle inequality, $\Vert a + b \Vert \le \Vert a \Vert + \Vert b \Vert$, which can both be easily proven.

How about areas and volumes? We just handle the case for $\R^3$ here, because higher dimension area or volume is hard to define. We may introduce the cross product $a \times b$, defined as $$ \begin{vmatrix} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ a_1 & a_2 & a_3 \\ b_1 & b_2 & b_3 \end{vmatrix}$$ Clearly $\times$ is bilinear and $b \times a = - a \times b$ directly from the properties of determinant. Similarly, we may define the triple product $a \cdot (b \times c)$ as $$ \begin{vmatrix} a_1 & a_2 & a_3 \\ b_1 & b_2 & b_3 \\ c_1 & c_2 & c_3 \end{vmatrix}$$ Also rely on the notion of determinant.

From elementary geometry we can deduce that if the inclined angle between $a$ and $b$ is $\theta$, then $a \cdot b = \Vert a \Vert \Vert b \Vert \cos \theta$ and $\Vert a \times b \Vert = \Vert a \Vert \Vert b \Vert \sin \theta$, so cross product $\Vert a \times b \Vert$ is the area of the parallelogram formed by $a$ and $b$. Note $a \times b \perp a, b$, so the triple product $(a \times b) \cdot c$ is actually the signed volume of the parallelopipe formed by $a$, $b$ and $c$.

Linear Objects

In the 2D plane everything is simple: We can either define lines in the form of linear equations $ax + by = c$ for $a, b, c \in \R$, or in parametric form $a + bt$ for $a, b \in \R^n$ and $t \in \R$. How can we translate those ideas into higher dimensions?

Actually it is pretty simple as well. We may define a hyperplane as set of points in the form $\{ x \in \R^n : a \cdot x = b \}$ where $a \in \R^n \setminus \{ 0 \}$ and $b \in \R$. Then, a linear object can be defined as intersection of hyperplanes. Linear algebra wise, then the dimension of the hyperplane is simply $n - k$ where $k$ is the rank of $A$ as in $A \cdot x = b$. Alternatively, it can also be represented similarly in the parametric form $a + b_1 t_1 + \cdots + b_k t_k$ with $\{ b_i \}$ being linear independent and $t_i \in \R$, representing a linear object of dimension $k$.

Curves

How about curves? We want to have a formal definition that encodes the intuitive definition of "put down a pen, move the pen, lift up the pen". Formally, a curve is a continuous function $x: I \rightarrow \R^n$ where $I \subset \R$ is interval. A curve $x: [a, b] \rightarrow \R^n$ is closed if $x(a) = x(b)$, and simple if $x(t_1) \ne x(t_2)$ for all $t_1 \lt t_2$ except at endpoints.

It is natural for us to extend the definition of limit and derivative from the single-variable cases as $\lim_{t \rightarrow a} x(t) = (\lim_{t \rightarrow a} x_1(t), \dots, \lim_{t \rightarrow a} x_n(t))$ and $x'(t) = \lim_{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{x(t + h) - x(t)}{h}$. We call $x'(t)$ the tangent vector of $x(t)$. Clearly $x'$ inherits all the single-variable rules.

How about the arclength of $\mathcal{C}^1$ (continuous-differentiable) curve $x$ for $a \le t \le b$? Intuitively, we may define the arclength $s$ as $\sup_{\{t_i\}} \Vert x(t_i) - x(t_{i - 1}) \Vert$, the supremum of the length of piecewise approximation, and equivalently $\int_{a}^b \Vert x'(t) \Vert \, dt$, noting $x(t_i) - x(t_{i - 1}) = x'(\xi) (t_i - t_{i - 1})$ for some $\xi \in (t_{i - 1}, t_i)$ by mean-value theorem.

Coordinate Systems

Other than the old-boring rectangular coordinates, sometimes we will handle points on circles, cylinder, spheres etc. How should we encode points in these coordinate systems?

First of all, we have the polar coordinates $(r, \theta)$ in $\R^2$, where $$\begin{cases} x = r \cos \theta \\ y = r \sin \theta \end{cases} \hspace{10mm} \begin{cases} r = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2} \\ \theta = \arctan \frac{y}{x} \end{cases}$$ Conventionally, we assume $r \in [0, \infty)$ and $\theta \in \R$. Intuitively, $r$ is the distance from the point to the origin while $\theta$ is the inclined angle.

Second, we have the cylindrical coordinates $(r, \theta, z)$ in $\R^3$, which is simply adding the third dimension, z-axis, to the polar coordinates.

A more complicated one is the spherical coordinates $(\rho, \theta, \phi)$, where $$\begin{cases} x = \rho \sin \phi \cos \theta \\ y = \rho \sin \phi \sin \theta \\ z = \rho \cos \phi \end{cases} \hspace{10mm} \begin{cases} \rho = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2 + z^2} \\ \theta = \arctan \frac{y}{x} \\ \phi = \arccos \frac{z}{\sqrt{x^2 + y^2 + z^2}}\end{cases}$$ Where essentially $\rho$ is the distance to origin, $\theta \in \R$ is the latitude and $\phi \in [0, \pi]$ is the longitude. This is especially useful when, well, handling spherical stuff.

Topology in Euclidean Space

In the euclidean space $\R^n$, we can define an open ball as $$B_\varepsilon(x_0) = \{ x \in \R^n : \Vert x - x_0 \Vert \lt \varepsilon \}$$ And a closed ball as $$\overline{B_\varepsilon(x_0)} = \{ x \in \R^n : \Vert x - x_0 \Vert \le \varepsilon \}$$ For $S \subset \R^n$, we define the interior of $S$ as $$ \text{Int}(S) := \{ x \in \R^n : B_\varepsilon(x) \subset S \text{ for some } \varepsilon \gt 0 \} $$ Similarly, we define the exterior of $S$ as $$ \text{Ext}(S) := \{ x \in \R^n : B_\varepsilon(x) \subset \R^n \setminus S \text{ for some } \varepsilon \gt 0 \} $$ Finally, the boundary of $S$ as $$ \partial S := \R^n \setminus (\text{Int}(S) \cup \text{Ext}(S))$$

Specifically, we call a set open when $S = \text{Int}(S)$, and closed when $S = \text{Int}(S) \cup \partial S$. We also define the closure of $S$ as $\overline{S} = S \cup \partial S$. Note that open and closed are not of opposite definitions; rather these are two related properties. Specially, $\R^n$ and $\varnothing$ are both open and closed, while set like $\mathbb{Q}$ are neither open or close in $\R$.

Finally, we also say $S \subset \R^n$ is bounded whenever there exists an $M$ where $S \subset B_M(0)$, and unbounded otherwise; And a set $S$ is connected whenever for all $x, y \in S$ there exists a curve connecting $x$ and $y$, and disconnected otherwise. The Jordan Curve Theorem states that a simple closed curve in $\mathbb{R}^2$ partition the region into two connected components, one bounded and one unbounded.

Functions in Euclidean Space

Generally, a scalar-valued multivariable function can be written as $f: \Omega \subset \R^n \rightarrow \R$, where $\Omega$ is the set where $f$ is defined over. Our target is to study these functions analytically, and to derive some general results.

Limit and Continuity

After introducing topological terminology, we can finally define limit and continuity of a function rigourously. What is the limit of a function $f : \Omega \subset \R^n \rightarrow \R$ at point $x \in \overline{\Omega}$, or what does it mean by $f$ is continuous at point $x \in \Omega$?

First, the limits. Intuitively, the statement $\lim_{x \rightarrow x_0} f(x) = L$ means that when $x$ approaches $x_0$, then $f(x)$ approaches $L$, where $f(x_0)$ not necessarily defined. How do we define "approaches"? There are actually two equivalent definitions: (1) $\varepsilon$-$\delta$: For every $\varepsilon \gt 0$, there exists $\delta \gt 0$ such that for all $x \in \Omega$ with $\Vert x - x_0 \Vert \lt \delta$, we have $\Vert f(x) - f(x_0) \Vert \lt \varepsilon$. (2) Sequential: For every sequence $\{ x_n \} \rightarrow x_0$, we have $\{ f(x_n) \} \rightarrow L$. Both can be shown to imply each other. The squeeze theorem states that for $f, g, h : \Omega \subset \R^n \rightarrow \R$ where $g(x) \le f(x) \le h(x)$ near $a \in \Omega$ and $\lim_{x \rightarrow a} g(x) = \lim_{x \rightarrow a} h(x) = L$, then $\lim_{x \rightarrow a} f(x) = L$ as well, which can be derive from definition.

Second, the continuity. We say $f$ is continuous at $x_0$ if and only if $\lim_{x \rightarrow x_0} f(x) = f(x_0)$ is well-defined, and the function $f$ itself is called continuous if $f$ is continuous at every point in $\Omega$. Clearly the set of functions continuous at $x_0$ is closed under addition, multiplication and division (by function not vanishes at $x_0$). Continuity in fact is also preserved by function composition, which can be shown by using chained $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ argument.

Partial Derivative

We want to achieve similar result as the 1D derivative: To approximate the function near a point with linear functions. The most natural thing is just to extend the definition of single-variable to multi-variable: For $f: \Omega \subset \R^n \rightarrow \R$ where $\Omega$ is open, define $\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_i} = f_{x_i} = D_{x_i} f = \lim_{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{f(x + h e_i) - f(x)}{h}$ where $e_i = (0, \dots, 1, \dots, 0)$ as the partial derivative of $f$ with respect to $x_i$. Note that the requirement for the set $\Omega$ being open is because we want $f(x + h e_i)$ where $h \rightarrow 0$ to be well-defined.

How about higher order derivatives? Naturally, we want to define like $f_{xy} = (f_x)_y = \frac{\partial}{\partial y} \left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\right) = \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y \partial x}$ (note the it is reversed due to function application order). A natural question is: does the order of the taking partial derivatives matter? For example, whether $f_{xy} = f_{yx}$ in general? If it is not true, then when does it holds?

Indeed, according to the Clairaut's Theorem / Mixed Derivative Theorem, $f_{xy} = f_{yx}$ whenever both $f_{xy}$ and $f_{yx}$ are well-defined and continuous in an open set, which can be proven with repeat application of Mean Value Theorem and simply "squeezing" the points.

How about more general cases? We call a function $\mathcal{C}^r$ if all partial derivates up to order $r$ are well-defined and continuous, and $\mathcal{C}^\infty$ or smooth if it is $\mathcal{C}^r$ for any $r \ge 0$. Specifically, a continuous function is $\mathcal{C}^0$. In general, if $f$ is $\mathcal{C}^r$, then the order of differentiation does not matter up to order $r$, since we may use clairaut to exchange adjacent partial derivative operators.

Differentiability

What does it means by $f$ is differentiable? One of the perspective to see this is that $f$ can be well-approximated by a linear function. Let $\nabla$ be the gradient operator $(D_{x_1}, \dots, D_{x_n})$, then the condition becomes whether $f(x) = f(x_0) + \nabla f (x_0) \cdot (x - x_0) + \varepsilon(x)$ where $\lim_{x \rightarrow a} \frac{\varepsilon(x)}{\Vert x - x_0 \Vert} = 0$, where $L(x) = f(x_0) + \nabla f (x_0) \cdot (x - x_0)$ is called the linearisation of $f$ near $x_0$. Clearly differentability implies continuity. Also, since the linearisation is good approximation, we can compute the directional derivative as $D_u f(x_0) = \lim_{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{f(x_0 + hu) - f(x_0)}{h} = \nabla f(x_0) \cdot u$ where $u$ is unit vector.

Interestingly, $\mathcal{C}^1$ implies differentiability on $\Omega$! This may be proven by simply splitting $x - x_0$ into components, then abuse the continuity of the partial derivatives. This is a quite useful property, since we may similarly extend to higher orders. We may define the total differential $df: \mathbb{R}^n \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ as well, as $df = \sum D_{x_i} dx_i$, considering differentials as functions.

Vector-valued functions are functions of the form $f: \Omega \subset \R^n \rightarrow \R^m$. Now, the range of the functions contains vectors instead of scalar. How shall we extend our analytic definitions to accomodate this?

Jacobian Matrix

Indeed, we can carry out linearisation on the vector-valued function similarly, where $f_i(x) = f_i(x_0) + \nabla f_i(x_0) \cdot (x - x_0) + \varepsilon_i(x)$. By writing $f$ as a column matrix (as convention), we have $ f(x) = f(x_0) + Df(x_0) (x - x_0) + \varepsilon(x)$ where $Df$ is the Jacobian Matrix $$ Df = \begin{bmatrix} \nabla f_1 \\ \nabla f_2 \\ \vdots \\ \nabla f_m \end{bmatrix}$$ Which clearly we have $df = Df \cdot dx$ as first-order linear approximations.

We also have the chain rule for multivariable: Simply described by $D(g \circ f)(a) = (Dg \circ f)(a) \cdot Df(a)$ Whenever $f$ and $g$ are differentiable at $a$ and $f(a)$ respectively, which can be proven with bounding the error of the linear approximation. This can be used to show that the for points $a$ in the level set $S = f^{-1}(c)$, $f$ differentiable at $a$ and $\nabla f (a) \ne 0$, then $\nabla f(a) \perp S$. That is, for every differentiable curve $\gamma$ on $S$ passing through $a$, we have $\nabla f(a) \cdot \gamma'(a) = 0$, which is true by $\nabla (f \circ \gamma) = 0$ and directly applying chain rule. We may as well use it to carry out implicit differentiations.

Finding Extrema

For a function $f : \Omega \subset \R^n \rightarrow \R$, we can define its global maximum and local maximum naturally, where $f$ has global maximum at $a$ iff $f(a) \ge f(x)$ for all $x \in \Omega$ and $f$ has local maximum at $a$ iff $f(a) \ge f(x)$ for all $x \in \Omega \cap B_{\varepsilon}(a)$ for some $\varepsilon > 0$. The case for minimum is just analogous.

When does a function has global maximum (and minimum)? For example, $f(x) = e^x$ on $\R$ does not have a global maximum nor minimum. According to the extreme value theorem, $f$ has global maximum and minimum whenever $\Omega$ is compact (closed and bounded) and $f$ continuous, since continuity preserves compactness and compact set (in $\mathbb{R}$) contains its supremum.

How can we find extrema then? The first derivative test states that if $f$ attains extremum at $a \in \text{Int}(\Omega)$, then $a$ is critical point, that is points where either the gradient is undefined or vanishes. Therefore, to find extrema, we may simply seek all the crtical points of $f$ in $\text{Int}(\Omega)$ and on the boundary $\partial \Omega$. For unbounded regions, a simple strategy is to simply first bound the region, then claim every point outside is obviously not going to be extrema with inequalities.
